# The CANON repo's own CI — Claudinite's test suite + its own conformance sweep
# on every PR. Not consumer wiring (consumers ship no workflow, #385).
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  # Dispatchable so a GITHUB_TOKEN-authored PR (whose push/open GitHub never
  # turns into a pull_request run — the recursion guard) can still get this
  # suite started on its branch: baselining's deliver() and any bot-authored
  # PR flow (#432, #565) dispatch it explicitly.
  workflow_dispatch:
defaults:
  run:
    shell: bash
jobs:
  test-and-conformance:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
          # Check out the PR's real head, not the synthetic refs/pull/N/merge commit
          # actions/checkout uses by default — otherwise HEAD is an ephemeral merge of
          # the branch into main, which the work-scoped squash-merge-history check would
          # (correctly, for that synthetic commit) flag. This makes CI evaluate exactly
          # what the local Stop hook does: the branch tip. Falls back to github.sha on push.
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.sha }}
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
      - name: Unit tests
        # THE test roots — a closed set of FOLDERS, each swept to any depth. Depth is
        # deliberately not enumerated: the previous form spelled out one glob per level of
        # nesting, so a test at an unlisted depth was silently never run — which is exactly
        # how vendoring/'s two files sat outside CI. `**` removes depth from the question;
        # what remains is the root list, and engine-tests/ci-test-roots.test.mjs fails the
        # moment a tracked test lands outside it. Adding a root is a deliberate CI edit;
        # adding a test is not.
        #   engine-tests/            engine/ (migrations included) + the other top-level canon code;
        #                            mirrors engine/'s inner structure, and stays canon-side
        #                            because engine/ ships to consumers exactly as-is (#385)
        #   packs/                   every canon pack's tests, each inside the pack it covers
        #   vendoring/               co-located with the vendor computer/writer they cover,
        #                            the fixture-consumer rehearsal included
        #   dev/tools/               maintainer-side tooling nothing at session time runs
        #   .claudinite/local/packs/ this repo's own local packs — tests live inside the tree
        # nullglob: a root with no tests drops out instead of reaching node as a literal pattern.
        run: |
          shopt -s globstar nullglob
          tests=(engine-tests/**/*.test.mjs packs/**/*.test.mjs vendoring/**/*.test.mjs dev/tools/**/*.test.mjs .claudinite/local/packs/**/*.test.mjs)
          # Deliberately oversubscribed. node --test defaults to one worker per core
          # minus one, which fits a CPU-bound suite; this one spends most of its wall
          # clock waiting — on git plumbing, spawned workers and converge fixtures — so
          # the cores idle at that default (measured on this tree: 106s wall against
          # 187s of user+sys on 4 cores). Doubling the workers: 106s -> 70s, with 16
          # buying only another 2s.
          #
          # TAP goes to a FILE, not the log. 2,448 tests emit ~13,000 lines at 5.3
          # lines each, and a failing run's one `not ok` sits wherever its file
          # finished — while GitHub's job-log API serves only a TAIL and the signed
          # blob URL that would serve the whole thing is proxy-blocked. So a red run
          # said `# fail 1` and nothing more, and five green local re-runs could not
          # name the test (#1170). Printing the failing blocks puts the identity in
          # the tail, where it can actually be read.
          status=0
          node --test --test-concurrency=$(( $(nproc) * 2 )) "${tests[@]}" > "$RUNNER_TEMP/tests.tap" || status=$?
          if [ "$status" -ne 0 ]; then
            echo '::group::failing tests'
            grep -n -A 25 '^not ok' "$RUNNER_TEMP/tests.tap" || echo 'no `not ok` line — the runner died before reporting one'
            echo '::endgroup::'
          fi
          tail -n 12 "$RUNNER_TEMP/tests.tap"
          exit "$status"
      - name: Conformance sweep (world scope)
        # The tree as it stands — the pattern bootstrap wires into consumers.
        run: node engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs
      - name: Conformance sweep (work scope)
        # The CHANGE, not the tree: this branch's diff against the base branch, the
        # only scope that can see what a commit did rather than what the repo now
        # holds. It used to run at the session's Stop hook and nowhere else, so a
        # rule about the change was enforced only where a session happened to be.
        #
        # The recipe — fetch the base, skip the engine's own branches, refuse an
        # empty scope, sweep — lives in the engine entry point, which every member
        # vendors and runs by the same one line. This repo is the one that runs it
        # from the repo root instead of the mount.
        #
        # --branch explicitly: the checkout above is a detached head at the PR's real
        # head sha, where `rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD` says "HEAD" and no branch name
        # is discoverable — so the skip for engine-authored branches would never fire.
        run: node engine/checks/ci-work-scope.mjs --branch "${{ github.head_ref || github.ref_name }}"
      - name: Growth write-surface gate
        # The lifecycle's capture runs (extract, dedup) are bounded to the repo's own
        # local packs. Unlike promote below, a capture run marks ITSELF — the pinned
        # commit subject its task doc gives it — so the gate self-gates and this step
        # runs on every PR, exiting 0 in ~no time on any other branch.
        run: node .claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/growth-scope-gate.mjs
      - name: Promote write-surface gate
        # The growth promote stage is the one change bounded to this canon's corpus roots — an
        # ordinary engine PR legitimately edits checks/ and engine/, so this cannot run on every
        # PR. It keys on the promote branch prefix (the task doc pins it) and fails the promote PR
        # if a changed path strays.
        if: contains(github.head_ref, 'growth-promote')
        run: node .claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/promote-scope-gate.mjs

defaults:
  run:
    shell: bash
jobs:
  test-and-conformance:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
          # Check out the PR's real head, not the synthetic refs/pull/N/merge commit
          # actions/checkout uses by default — otherwise HEAD is an ephemeral merge of
          # the branch into main, which the work-scoped squash-merge-history check would
          # (correctly, for that synthetic commit) flag. This makes CI evaluate exactly
          # what the local Stop hook does: the branch tip. Falls back to github.sha on push.
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.sha }}
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
      - name: Unit tests
        # THE test roots — a closed set of FOLDERS, each swept to any depth. Depth is
        # deliberately not enumerated: the previous form spelled out one glob per level of
        # nesting, so a test at an unlisted depth was silently never run — which is exactly
        # how vendoring/'s two files sat outside CI. `**` removes depth from the question;
        # what remains is the root list, and engine-tests/ci-test-roots.test.mjs fails the
        # moment a tracked test lands outside it. Adding a root is a deliberate CI edit;
        # adding a test is not.
        #   engine-tests/            engine/ (migrations included) + the other top-level canon code;
        #                            mirrors engine/'s inner structure, and stays canon-side
        #                            because engine/ ships to consumers exactly as-is (#385)
        #   packs/                   every canon pack's tests, each inside the pack it covers
        #   vendoring/               co-located with the vendor computer/writer they cover,
        #                            the fixture-consumer rehearsal included
        #   dev/tools/               maintainer-side tooling nothing at session time runs
        #   .claudinite/local/packs/ this repo's own local packs — tests live inside the tree
        # nullglob: a root with no tests drops out instead of reaching node as a literal pattern.
        run: |
          shopt -s globstar nullglob
          tests=(engine-tests/**/*.test.mjs packs/**/*.test.mjs vendoring/**/*.test.mjs dev/tools/**/*.test.mjs .claudinite/local/packs/**/*.test.mjs)
          # Deliberately oversubscribed. node --test defaults to one worker per core
          # minus one, which fits a CPU-bound suite; this one spends most of its wall
          # clock waiting — on git plumbing, spawned workers and converge fixtures — so
          # the cores idle at that default (measured on this tree: 106s wall against
          # 187s of user+sys on 4 cores). Doubling the workers: 106s -> 70s, with 16
          # buying only another 2s.
          #
          # TAP goes to a FILE, not the log. 2,448 tests emit ~13,000 lines at 5.3
          # lines each, and a failing run's one `not ok` sits wherever its file
          # finished — while GitHub's job-log API serves only a TAIL and the signed
          # blob URL that would serve the whole thing is proxy-blocked. So a red run
          # said `# fail 1` and nothing more, and five green local re-runs could not
          # name the test (#1170). Printing the failing blocks puts the identity in
          # the tail, where it can actually be read.
          status=0
          node --test --test-concurrency=$(( $(nproc) * 2 )) "${tests[@]}" > "$RUNNER_TEMP/tests.tap" || status=$?
          if [ "$status" -ne 0 ]; then
            echo '::group::failing tests'
            grep -n -A 25 '^not ok' "$RUNNER_TEMP/tests.tap" || echo 'no `not ok` line — the runner died before reporting one'
            echo '::endgroup::'
          fi
          tail -n 12 "$RUNNER_TEMP/tests.tap"
          exit "$status"
      - name: Conformance sweep (world scope)
        # The tree as it stands — the pattern bootstrap wires into consumers.
        run: node engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs
      - name: Conformance sweep (work scope)
        # The CHANGE, not the tree: this branch's diff against the base branch, the
        # only scope that can see what a commit did rather than what the repo now
        # holds. It used to run at the session's Stop hook and nowhere else, so a
        # rule about the change was enforced only where a session happened to be.
        #
        # The recipe — fetch the base, skip the engine's own branches, refuse an
        # empty scope, sweep — lives in the engine entry point, which every member
        # vendors and runs by the same one line. This repo is the one that runs it
        # from the repo root instead of the mount.
        #
        # --branch explicitly: the checkout above is a detached head at the PR's real
        # head sha, where `rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD` says "HEAD" and no branch name
        # is discoverable — so the skip for engine-authored branches would never fire.
        run: node engine/checks/ci-work-scope.mjs --branch "${{ github.head_ref || github.ref_name }}"
      - name: Growth write-surface gate
        # The lifecycle's capture runs (extract, dedup) are bounded to the repo's own
        # local packs. Unlike promote below, a capture run marks ITSELF — the pinned
        # commit subject its task doc gives it — so the gate self-gates and this step
        # runs on every PR, exiting 0 in ~no time on any other branch.
        run: node .claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/growth-scope-gate.mjs
      - name: Promote write-surface gate
        # The growth promote stage is the one change bounded to this canon's corpus roots — an
        # ordinary engine PR legitimately edits checks/ and engine/, so this cannot run on every
        # PR. It keys on the promote branch prefix (the task doc pins it) and fails the promote PR
        # if a changed path strays.
        if: contains(github.head_ref, 'growth-promote')
        run: node .claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/promote-scope-gate.mjs

# Searching for a tool

- **A search that finds nothing** is evidence about your query, not about the environment: vary
  the query before concluding a capability is absent, and try the tool before telling the owner a
  step is theirs.
- **`select:` takes a short name as readily as a qualified one** — `select:get_teams` and
  `select:mcp__github__get_teams` both return the tool, and a comma-separated list loads several at
  once. Qualify a name two servers could both carry. (1)
- **A bare short name is a keyword query, and resolves too** — `get_teams` on its own returns the
  tool, ranked above the looser matches beneath it.
- **A server whose whole roster the deferred-tools listing already names** is the one exception: one
  miss there is the answer, so read the roster rather than rephrase the query.

S1 (#1478) moved queue/create-work-item.mjs and converge-workflows.mjs and
swept the canon's own docs to their new homes. A converge refreshes
.claudinite/shared/ alone, so the copies members took into their own
.claudinite/local/packs/** went on naming paths the next vendor set no longer
carried — a BLOCKING runnable-doc-commands finding in a repository no canon
session reads. Shepherd's update failed at three of them.

Both paths come back as runnable entry shims over the real modules, so a
holder's prose resolves again at the next converge with nobody editing
anything. They are tolerances rather than this folder's ABI — the prose
holding them open is markdown a member can edit, where a .github/workflows/
is not — so each carries @legacy-tolerance retire:#2048, and each prints,
when the old path is run, the one thing a check cannot deliver: the new path,
to the holder, by name.

The assurance is a history walk, sibling to the engine-lane scan: every mount
path any fielded canon doc told a member to run must still resolve. It is
quantified over the trunk's doc history rather than HEAD, because HEAD's docs
are exactly the copies a move sweeps. It found both paths red before the
shims, and a third the growth pack's rename left behind (#2050), tracked
rather than waived.

Refs #2049 #2048 #2050

Eight corpus claims about the environment no longer held when re-probed in a
live session; every verdict, corrected or not, is in the pull request body with
the probe behind it.

The largest: the sandbox's egress proxy now authenticates api.github.com as the
session's own GitHub identity, so a repo inside the session's scope answers 200
with no Authorization header and only a repo outside it 403s. Six places stated
the blanket 403, "no REST credential", or "carries no repo token". Relatedly,
git ls-remote reaches a repo the REST API refuses, so four task docs justifying
"never a cross-repo checkout" with "the sandbox has no cross-repo git" now say
the boundary is the session's granted scope.

Also: select: resolves a short name now, retiring a split whose references entry
named exactly that condition; Edit's read requirement binds only outside the
working directory and the session scratchpad, where a shell write does not
satisfy it; list_workflow_jobs and download_workflow_run_artifact readdressed as
methods of actions_list and actions_get; and unattended-agents' rule holds but
not by the symptom it named, GITHUB_TOKEN being set-but-empty and node's global
fetch going direct, so the failure arrives as an IP-keyed rate-limit 403.

Eleven claims re-probed and held, four named unprobed rather than guessed at.
Two holders of the same stale fact sit in .claudinite/local/packs/, outside this
task's corpus, and are reported for the local-pack lane instead.

entries.name: mcp__github__actions_get
entries.description:
Get details about specific GitHub Actions resources.
Use this tool to get details about individual workflows, workflow runs, jobs, and artifacts by their unique IDs.

resource_id.description:
The unique identifier of the resource. This will vary based on the "method" provided, so ensure you provide the correct ID:
- Provide a workflow ID or workflow file name (e.g. ci.yaml) for 'get_workflow' method.
- Provide a workflow run ID for 'get_workflow_run', 'get_workflow_run_usage', and 'get_workflow_run_logs_url' methods.
- Provide an artifact ID for 'download_workflow_run_artifact' method.
- Provide a job ID for 'get_workflow_job' method.

entries.name: mcp__github__actions_list
entries.description:
Tools for listing GitHub Actions resources.
Use this tool to list workflows in a repository, or list workflow runs, jobs, and artifacts for a specific workflow or workflow run.

perPage.description: Results per page for pagination (default: 30, max: 100)

resource_id.description:
The unique identifier of the resource. This will vary based on the "method" provided, so ensure you provide the correct ID:
- Do not provide any resource ID for 'list_workflows' method.
- Provide a workflow ID or workflow file name (e.g. ci.yaml) for 'list_workflow_runs' method, or omit to list all workflow runs in the repository.
- Provide a workflow run ID for 'list_workflow_jobs' and 'list_workflow_run_artifacts' methods.

filter.description: Filters jobs by their completed_at timestamp

workflow_jobs_filter.description: Filters for workflow jobs. **ONLY** used when method is 'list_workflow_jobs'

actor.description: Filter to a specific GitHub user's workflow runs.

branch.description: Filter workflow runs to a specific Git branch. Use the name of the branch.

event.description: Filter workflow runs to a specific event type

status.description: Filter workflow runs to only runs with a specific status

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/writing-tests

# Testing practices

A consuming repo's own test *mechanics* — runner, layout, which suites exist — are its own docs'; CI-trigger rules and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` workflow-recursion gotcha are [git-github-advanced](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md)'s.

- See a test fail before you trust it: write it red before the fix (green after), or break what it guards and watch it go red. A test that has never failed proves nothing. For a **refusal/negative** test — one asserting a guard yields *nothing* — the write-it-red-first branch is unavailable: the pre-change code also yielded nothing, so the test passes from birth and proves nothing. See-it-fail there **must** be the second method — mutate the new guard (weaken it), watch the test bite, then restore it. Restore with `git checkout -- <file>` (or `git stash`) taken at the moment of mutating — never a `.bak` copy saved earlier, which predates whatever else you edited in between and silently discards that intervening work. If the mutation was **staged** (to make a check that scans `git diff --cached` fire), a bare `git checkout -- <file>` restores from the index — which now holds the mutation — so the "restore" is a no-op; use `git checkout HEAD -- <file>` (or `git reset` first).
- A mechanism meant to survive a retry, re-queue, or hand-off needs a test that calls it twice, not once. A suite of single-call tests stays green while the multi-call case corrupts state — the double-call is what a real retry, requeue, or hand-off actually does. When the mechanism arbitrates by identity (a claim, a lock), the second call must come from a **different actor**: a single actor retrying its own stale claim can't expose an identity-masked race, since it still recognizes its own claim as valid.
- A simulator of a stateful mechanism must advance state only where the real engine's code actually leaves a mark — never wherever the rule's stated description says a transition happens. A sim that fires on every event matching the rule's *intent* is correct by construction against that rule and blind to exactly the silent paths where the real implementation and the rule have quietly diverged — which is where a genuine bug usually lives. Read the real engine's code for what it *writes*, and model that.
- Before trusting a new transform/normalizer, run it over the *real existing corpus* it will process, not just hand-picked test inputs — the live data exposes edge cases your examples won't. Relatedly, prefer a generic structural rule over a hand-maintained list of special cases: the enumerated list needs per-instance upkeep and silently has gaps, while a rule keyed on structure (e.g. "a known registry label under any 2-letter ccTLD") covers the whole class at once. (3)
- A test that stubs the exact boundary where the bug lives can't catch that bug — it guards only the shape it asserts, not the runtime effect. Say what it can't catch.
- A test that dereferences a path inside a **read-only dependency tree someone else refreshes** — a vendored mount, a synced submodule, generated output from an upstream build — is a test whose fixture a stranger can delete: the day upstream retires that file the case fails `ENOENT` with nothing in your repo having changed. Assert against a path only when the test itself creates it; when a case genuinely needs an upstream file, read it **defensively** and skip with a stated reason if it is gone, so a retirement upstream reports as "no longer applicable" rather than as your repo being broken. Check what actually runs these cases too — a suite that the repo's own gate never invokes reports its breakage to whoever happens to look.
- **Never test that a value is set.** A test that reads a value someone declared — a config or manifest field (`assert.equal(task.expected_outcome, 'fresh_pr')`), an exported constant or default object (`assert.deepEqual(DEFAULTS, {…})`), a settings file naming a pack, a workflow's `run:` line, a frontmatter key — and asserts it is the literal it was set to restates the file under test in a second file. It can only fail when someone changes the value **on purpose**, so it catches no defect and instead taxes every deliberate change with a mirrored edit — and teaches that the value is load-bearing prose to be restated, which is how one setting ends up copied into a comment, a worker doc, a README table and a test, so flipping it becomes a five-file diff. The see-it-fail test exposes it: to make the assertion go red you must break the thing it asserts, which is not a bug. "It exists", "it has the right shape" and "it is one of these" are the same test in a looser coat. Test the **behaviour the value drives** instead: feed the real code the declared value and assert what the code does with it — a task declared `weekly` is planned once across a fourteen-day clock, a check declared over `**/*.mjs` fires on a fixture `.mjs` and stays silent on a `.md`, a default object yields the documented output when nothing overrides it. Where no code reads the value there is nothing to test; if a declaration genuinely must not change without deliberation, that is a review concern, not a test. What *does* earn an assertion on declared data is a claim spanning two artifacts that could drift independently: the doc a field *names* exists; every signal the code reads is declared; two implementations of the same list agree; a value the runtime constrains is inside its legal set — proven by running the constraint, not by re-listing the set.
- **Testing a task's precondition or declaration** — assert only the pack's own code: a
  task-local term's decisions, a worker's behaviour, or a composition it designed; a plain
  built-in term or a validated declaration is the scheduler's own mechanism, proved once by its
  own suite.
- Prefer a single shared double; but when a subsystem is faked by more than one (a minimal unit stub vs. a faithful harness that boots the real module), a new call into the faked surface must be taught to **every** double, or the untaught one breaks — and the faithful harness turns an unmodeled API into a confusing **far-away** failure (a DOM-snapshot pixel-diff, not a local error at the call site). After adding a call into a faked boundary, find every double of it and extend each.
- When one wire format, encoding, or algorithm is **implemented twice** — two languages, two tiers, a hand-rolled client encoder against the server's library — no compiler, type system, or single test run spans the two, so the only thing holding them together is a **shared vector set carried deliberately by both suites**: the same inputs and the same expected outputs, asserted independently on each side, including the boundary cases the two could plausibly round differently (a value exactly on a bisection midpoint, a tie, a truncation edge). A vector asserted on only one side is an input nobody ever compared — both suites stay green, in different languages under different runners, while the claim quietly stops covering it. So: touching *either* implementation re-runs *both* suites, and adding a vector adds it to both. Where the pairing is mechanical (the two vector lists must contain the same inputs), pin it with a check rather than a convention.
- A traceability/coverage gate that requires every spec item be *claimed* by some test of one fixed kind proves only that it's claimed, not that it's verified. When items differ in kind, the gate green-lights claims that kind can't check — a pixel snapshot "covers" a click's tab-opening it can never observe, or a state the case never renders (and can't, when the data can't reach it). Segment the gate by the verification each item needs (route behavior to a behavior test, rendering to a snapshot) rather than forcing every item onto one mechanism. (1)
- A golden/snapshot test whose expected artifact is hand-authored to mirror what production renders is a parallel implementation: it drifts from the real output and can't catch changes to the renderer (a hand-built UI gallery even faked a state the app never shows). Drive the snapshot through the real code path, faking only its inputs.
- A snapshot/golden test that depends on the current date/time must inject a fixed reference instant, not read the real clock — else a fixed-date fixture silently rots as wall-clock time passes ("this year" becomes "past" next year). Thread the reference time through the code under test, defaulting to the real clock in production. When retrofitting such a rule into an existing fixture suite, pin the reference instant so existing fixtures land on the same side they were authored for — so only the cases that deliberately exercise the new rule change and the diff stays small and reviewable, rather than a sprawling baseline churn that buries the intended change.
- A round-trip test that asserts by comparing **serialized** forms (`JSON.stringify(decoded) === JSON.stringify(original)`) silently makes key *order* part of the contract: add a field at the top of the encoder's record and append it in the decoder's, and the round-trip fails on ordering alone — with a diff that reads like a data bug and sends you after a value that was correct all along. Deep-equal the parsed structures instead, so the test states what it means; keep serialized comparison only where byte-identity is genuinely the property under test, and say so in the test.
- A new **e2e / heavy-browser** test must go green at least twice in CI before merging — one green run doesn't rule out a flake. This applies only to that class (the real-Chrome `test/fullBrowserHeavyTests/` suites); the deterministic offline/unit/integration tests don't touch a live browser or network, so one green run is enough for them.
- A test that can only run remotely (e.g. CI-only) must diagnose itself: on failure, dump the observed state, not just an assertion. It must also be *hang-proof* — bound every `await` (a timeout race) and set a test-level timeout — so a failure fails fast with that diagnostic instead of burning the whole job's timeout. An unbounded await on something that never settles (e.g. a callback that silently never fires) turns a 5-second failure into a 20-minute hang, and each CI-only iteration already costs a full round-trip.
- Run a suite you know is slow as **its own command with an explicit timeout well above its measured runtime**, and do the dependency install as a *separate, earlier* call. An agent shell caps a command at a default (order of a couple of minutes) and pushes it to the background when it expires; the reflex is then to start the suite over, so one green result costs double the wall clock with two suites racing each other. Chaining setup in front of the suite is what usually pushes the pair past the cap. If a run does get backgrounded, wait on the one already running rather than launching a second.
- To test code that drives a real browser or other external runtime in CI, prefer a *self-authored hermetic input* (e.g. a `data:` URL whose own script reproduces the behavior) over hitting a live third-party target — the live target is non-deterministic and often bot-blocked from a CI/datacenter IP, so it flakes or can't run, while a self-authored input exercises the same engine deterministically. (2)
- Gate a fuzzy quality metric (a coverage %, not a binary pass) behind a high-watermark: refresh the artifact and ratchet the watermark up locally, keep CI read-only (assert against the committed baseline, never rewrite it), and re-baseline by hand only when a deliberate change legitimately moves it — a number that can only climb catches a silent regression without flapping on noise. When the population it covers can *grow* (e.g. new test cases), store the set the watermark was computed over and gate only over the cases shared with it, so a newly added item is excluded rather than dragging the aggregate below the bar; re-anchor the watermark when the set changes. (A single aggregate watermark can then be re-anchored over a regression bundled into the *same* change as a set change — store per-item bars if that must be caught.)
- For behavior a person must sign off on (a third-party integration, an extraction result), keep a layer of declarative, human-reviewed expectation files — distinct from the unit tests, which nobody reads for *intent* — and cover every behavior change with a minimal, representative case there (one behavior per case, no incidental complexity), since that case is what gets reviewed.
- When a snapshot/golden test fails because the output *legitimately* moved (the pixels or bytes changed for a real reason), don't quietly regenerate the baseline to go green — an unreviewed baseline change is an unreviewed behavior change. Surface the diff (committed **expected**, newly-rendered **actual**, highlighted **diff**) and get owner approval before re-baselining; until then keep the *reverted* baseline committed so the branch honestly shows the test red-pending — never commit the new baseline first.
- When a test asserts exact values extracted from a captured artifact (a cached page, a recorded response), record and commit the artifact *first*, then read the expected values off the committed file — don't hand-write the expectations from memory or a live view and hope they match. Guessing the value desyncs the test from the real fixture; reading it off the committed bytes can't.
- A test that maintains a committed artifact should regenerate it into the working tree deterministically (no timestamps, so an unchanged run yields no diff) and skip the write under CI — never shell out to git from a test. Commit the artifact through the normal review flow, like a snapshot.
- Render a UI *image* golden with the engine that matches the surface, and prefer the deterministic one. A surface that is inline-styled SVG, or flexbox-only markup authored for it, renders **bit-exact** through a headless rasterizer (e.g. satori → SVG, resvg → PNG) driven by the shipped code, using **bundled** fonts, never system fonts, and a pinned locale — demand a **zero-pixel** diff there. But that rasterizer has no CSS engine and draws no native widgets: a full shipped page using CSS **grid**, custom properties (`var()`), `@media`, **emoji**, or **form controls** (a range slider, radio, `<select>`) is beyond it — screenshot that with a **headless browser** instead, and allow a *small* diff tolerance (browser antialiasing varies across machines, so it isn't bit-exact). Match the engine to the surface; never reshape the product to fit the rasterizer. (A rasterized popup golden works only because the popup was authored flexbox-only — the moment a surface needs grid/vars/widgets, it needs a browser.) Since the browser goldens aren't gate-able bit-exact and a runner may lack the browser, let those cases **self-skip** where it's absent so the deterministic cases still gate.
- Reproduce a reported golden-image flake with the harness's own pixel comparator, never a raw byte or file-hash compare: a byte-hash is strictly tighter than a zero-pixel-diff comparator (it also fails on identical pixels re-encoded differently), so it manufactures "reproductions" of a flake that never fails the real gate.
- To image-golden a surface your code **injects into a host page** (a control mounted into a third-party toolbar), render it against a **committed capture of the real host DOM with its computed styles flattened inline** — the deterministic rasterizer reads only inline styles, and the host's own stylesheet is not yours to ship. Mount it with the **shipped injector** (so the golden proves the placement, not a hand-placed copy), and name the model's boundary honestly: substituted icon-font glyphs, an approximated host chrome (a captured sample is spec, not folklore — the origin lesson of a supported-targets matrix).

# Committing

- **One concern per commit.** If two changes could each stand alone, split them; a message that
  wants numbered items is the split talking.
- **Reference the issue, when the change has one** — `Refs #n`, or `Fixes #n` / `Closes #n` where
  the commit finishes it. A change tracked by its PR alone references nothing.
- **A landed commit is revised by a new commit**, never a rewrite of that one.
- **Stage by name** — `git add <paths>` for the files this commit is about; `-a` sweeps in whatever
  else was in progress.

# Writing a check that scans the repo

- **Choosing the file set** — take it from `git ls-files` rather than a filesystem walk with
  paths to skip, and remember a brand-new file is untracked until you add it, so a green run
  isn't coverage of it.

- **Scanning for a forbidden token** — strip comments first so it matches code, not prose —
  string-aware, since a `//` inside a URL is not a comment. Reuse `stripComments` from
  [`engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs`](../../../../engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs);
  if the scan can't import it, inline the same pass and point a comment back at that source.
  Strip in **both** directions — a comment that documents or warns about the banned pattern is
  exactly where a naive check trips over its own reasoning, so a commented-out instance must not
  count as present either.

- **Proving the check silent** — run it against the repo's own **real** sources, not only a
  synthetic clean fixture — a fixture spelling the same gap the check has just keeps proving the
  matching, and only a real-tree run can disagree with you.

git add engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs engine/checks/check_the_work.mjs && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Let the check runners' output survive their exit

`check_the_world.mjs --list` could hand a caller a catalog cut off at a row
boundary — exit status 0, empty stderr, a silently short answer on the channel
whose whole purpose is being machine-read. Measured on origin/main with six
cores busy, 15 of 60 spawnSync callers got a partial catalog, each missing a
tail of 6-9 rules; the suite's own --list test caught it once in two runs and
read as a flake.

The cause is process.exit() over a PIPE. Every caller that CAPTURES the output
— a test's spawnSync, a shell pipeline, an Actions step — gets a pipe, where a
Node write is asynchronous, and process.exit() discards whatever is still
queued. Under load the event loop has not drained it yet, so the tail is simply
lost. Nothing reports this: the status was already decided.

Both runners now set process.exitCode and let the process end on its own, which
flushes. The world runner's branches become an if/else chain, since an exit code
does not stop the script the way process.exit did, and the catalog goes out as
one write rather than one per rule.

The same hazard sits on the other entry points that print before exiting
(selftest, converge-wiring, the migration runner and ~120 further call sites);
their outputs are small, and the sweep over them is filed separately.

Under the identical load, 60 of 60 runs now return the full catalog.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01TazEpVGd2ZXhBg3okvQeot
EOF
git log --oneline -1

git add engine-tests/helpers.mjs engine/checks/helpers/repo-context.mjs && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Cut the git subprocesses every check fixture pays for

A ruleTester case is a fixed cost paid over a thousand times in this suite:
makeRepo seeds a scratch repo, buildContext reads it, and between them that was
seventeen git subprocesses and 53ms before a single rule ran — the broad band
the per-test distribution is made of, not a few slow outliers.

Two of those seventeen spawns are the fixture's own content; the rest are
setup that is identical every time.

makeRepo now seeds ONE template repo per process and copies it. `git init` plus
the seed commit plus the feature branch produces a byte-identical tree for every
fixture whose `base` is empty, which is nearly all of them, and a file copy of
the result is ~3ms against ~27ms of subprocesses. The template is pruned of the
ten files git writes there and never reads back — the hook samples above all —
which was four fifths of the copy. A fixture with its own `base` files needs
them in the seed commit and still seeds the long way.

resolveBaseRef asked `rev-parse --verify` once per candidate and stopped at the
first hit, so a repo whose base is a local `main` — every check fixture, and any
clone with no remote — paid two misses on the `origin/` candidates before its
answer. `cat-file --batch-check` takes all four on stdin and answers each
independently through the same revision parser, `^{commit}` peeling included, in
one spawn. Verified to agree with rev-parse on every ambiguity that separates
them: a tag sharing a branch's name, a remote-tracking ref with no local branch,
both spellings present, and the canon checkout itself.

makeRepo 23.4ms -> 11.4ms, buildContext 28.9ms -> 23.3ms, a case 53.2ms ->
35.3ms. Proven behaviour-identical rather than assumed: the whole context —
every field, every file's contents, the added lines, the vendored set — hashes
the same through the old and new seeding paths across eight fixture shapes in
both scopes, including .gitignore/.gitattributes cases.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01TazEpVGd2ZXhBg3okvQeot
EOF
git log --oneline -3 && git status --short

input.title: Halve the test suite: unblock the long pole, cut the per-fixture git spawns
input.body:
Ran the `ci-performance-evaluation` playbook end to end over this repo's suite.

**Local: 120.6s → 57-60s** (3667 tests, all green, three runs each arm, 4 cores).
CI's `Unit tests` step is the number to watch — it was 116-129s across recent runs and is 86-90% of the whole job.

## Where the time actually was

The step breakdown first, over several runs: checkout 9-10s, setup-node 5s, **Unit tests 116-129s**, all three sweeps and both gates together ≤1s. So the tests, and nothing else, were the job.

Locally the suite ran 120.6s wall against 250s of user+sys on 4 cores — **52% utilisation, three cores idle**. Timing every file on its own found why:

| | |
|---|---|
| serial total, all 301 files | 263s |
| `vendoring/rehearsal/rehearsal.test.mjs` alone | **76.5s** |
| perfect 4-core parallelism would give | 66s |

`node --test` parallelises across *files*, so that one file's 76.5s was a floor no number of workers could get under — and it was above the ideal, which is exactly why the suite sat at 120s with cores to spare. Everything else was a broad band of ~1000 tests at a near-identical 53ms each: a fixed fixture cost, not slow tests.

## What changed

**1. The rehearsals run concurrently.** The 74 (fixture, mode) rehearsals in that one file each spend their wall clock waiting on nine child processes and share nothing — own temp dir, own subprocesses. `step()`/`buildFixture()` become async and the tests sit in a `describe` with a measured concurrency of 4. Steps *within* one rehearsal stay strictly ordered, each awaiting the last, because each judges what the one before wrote.

File alone **79.1s → 22.1s**; the 78.7s of CPU it now spends over 22.1s wall is 3.6 of 4 cores, so 4 is at the knee, not below it. Proven still able to fail: pointing a step at a missing module turns the rehearsals red with the failing step's output intact.

**2. The per-fixture cost.** A `ruleTester` case was 17 git subprocesses and 53ms before a single rule ran.
- `makeRepo` seeds one template repo per process and copies it. `git init` + seed commit + feature branch is byte-identical for every fixture with an empty `base` — nearly all of them — and a file copy is ~3ms against ~27ms of subprocesses. The template is pruned of the ten files git writes and never reads back (the hook samples above all), which was four fifths of the copy.
- `resolveBaseRef` asked `rev-parse --verify` once per candidate, so a repo based on a local `main` — every fixture, and any clone with no remote — paid two `origin/` misses first. `cat-file --batch-check` answers all four on stdin in one spawn, through the same revision parser.

makeRepo 23.4ms → 11.4ms, buildContext 28.9ms → 23.3ms, **a case 53.2ms → 35.3ms**.

Behaviour-identical rather than assumed to be: the whole context — every field, file contents, added lines, the vendored set — hashes the same through both seeding paths across eight fixture shapes in both scopes; and `cat-file` agrees with `rev-parse` on every ambiguity that separates them (a tag sharing a branch's name, a remote ref with no local branch, both spellings present, the canon checkout itself).

## A real bug the faster suite surfaced

One of the A/B runs went red on `--list emits the machine-readable rule catalog`. Not a flake: the catalog was cut off after the `t` rules, missing exactly the last 8. On **pristine `origin/main`**, with six cores busy, **15 of 60 `spawnSync` callers got a partial catalog** — status 0, empty stderr, a silently short answer on the channel whose whole purpose is being machine-read.

The cause is `process.exit()` over a pipe: every caller that *captures* output gets one, a Node pipe write is asynchronous, and `process.exit()` drops what is still queued. Both check runners now set `process.exitCode` and let the process end, which flushes; the world runner's branches become an if/else chain since an exit code does not stop the script, and the catalog goes out as one write. Under the identical load, **60 of 60 now return the full catalog**.

The same hazard sits on ~120 further `process.exit` call sites that print first (selftest, converge-wiring, the migration runner). Their outputs are small; that sweep is filed separately rather than widened into this PR.

## Left alone deliberately

- **Merging `buildContext`'s two `git diff --name-only` calls into one `--name-status`** — worth ~3ms a case, but the two disagree on rename entries in ways a fixture would not show, and it is not worth a subtle scoping bug.
- **Making `ctx.commits` / `ctx.branch` lazy** — another ~5ms a case. Real, but the suite is now within 10% of its 4-core floor, so it would buy single-digit seconds against a change to engine code every member runs.
- **Setup and install time in CI** — checkout 9-10s, setup-node 5s. There is no lockfile and no install step; nothing to cache.
- The 1562 tests that already run in under 1ms are 0.1% of the suite. They are fine, and this says so, so nobody re-profiles them.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/do-later

# /do-later — defer a change into a chained request run

File the deferred change as an **ad-hoc request**: an issue the
queue picks up on its own, held behind what is still in flight — never an ordinary issue,
which waits for somebody to remember it.

You are filing work, not doing it. Touch no source file, open no branch.

## What you write

**One issue, well defined.** The run that implements it will never see this
conversation — the issue body is the whole brief. State the change, the files or
surfaces it touches if you know them, what "done" looks like, and anything the
owner ruled out. Size it to its idea; a rename is a sentence.

**Every field a run reads is one block on the first lines of the description**,
above the marker and ahead of your prose — the waits and the parameters together,
verbatim in this spelling:

```
Blocked-by: #<what this waits on>
Not-before: <ISO instant this may first run>
Model: <opus | sonnet | haiku>
Automerge: <policy>
Task: <pack>/<task>

<!-- filed by /do-later -->

<the brief>
```

Write only the lines the deferral actually has; each is explained below. A field
further down the body still parses, but nobody editing the issue can then see what
the run will do, and a retry that rewrites `Not-before:` has no one place to write
it. (1)

The two waits compose: an issue carrying both sleeps until every blocker has
closed **and** the moment has passed.

**What issue it waits on**, first match wins:

1. the issue of the **previous `/do-later` you filed in this session** — that is
   the chain the owner asked for, each deferral behind the last;
2. otherwise the **pull request** the session's work is on, if one is open;
3. otherwise the **issue** the session is working on;
4. otherwise nothing — omit the field, and say in your reply that it queues
   immediately.

Only ever name blockers that will actually *close* — a merged PR does, a branch
does not. If you filed an earlier `/do-later` this session but no longer have its
number, find it by its marker line among the repo's open issues rather than
falling back to (2).

**What moment it waits on.** A deferral the owner words as a *time* — "check
tomorrow", "in a week", "not until after the release" — waits on an instant, and
`Blocked-by:` cannot express it. That is `Not-before:`, and it is the queue's own
wait field rather than a parameter: it is honoured whether or not the author holds
push access. Give it an ISO-8601 instant resolved against today's date
(`Not-before: 2026-08-28T09:00:00Z`) — the next scheduler run adopts the issue,
holds it blocked, and releases it on the first hourly pass after that instant.
A time-worded deferral is never case 4: it waits on the moment even when no issue
or PR is in flight, so it does not "queue immediately".

## The mark, and the parameters in the body

**The mark is one label**: **`task:origin:ad-hoc`** (`mcp__github__issue_write`,
`labels`). The next scheduler run adopts the issue — writing its machine block
into the body and giving it a status — and the issue itself becomes the work
item, so the whole run plays out where the owner is already looking. Nothing else
is a label any more; everything below rides the issue **body**, and is honoured
only for an author with push access on the repository.

- **`Model: <family>`** — the family **this** session is running, so the deferred
  work is done by what the owner is working with now. Read it with `get_session`
  (claude-code-remote, `session_id` omitted) and map `session_context.model` to
  `opus`, `sonnet` or `haiku`. A model outside those three is left out, and the
  run takes the task's default.
- **`Automerge: <policy>`** — the standing authorization to land the change
  without the owner's approval **when the run's diff turns out to sit inside the
  policy** (the run measures this with the policy engine, not you). The value is
  a policy expression: `anything`, a `;`-joined list of diff classes — built-ins
  like `comment-only-changes`, `doc-changes`, `test-changes`,
  `markdown-line-removals`, `markdown-trims`, `file-additions`, `generated-file-changes`, `javascript-changes`,
  `single-file-code-changes`, `single-folder-code-changes`, plus any class the
  repo's packs declare — each optionally `reject:`-prefixed, or `narrow-diff`
  (docs, tests, comment-only edits, and code within a single directory). A term
  can also name a folder inline, `under:<dir>` — any change of any kind inside
  that directory, and nothing outside it. Listing terms *widens* (a file need
  only match one); `&&` inside a term narrows, every part having to match:
  `under:docs && doc-changes`.

  **This field is never left unsettled, and never defaulted silently.** If the
  owner stated a policy, or said they want to see this one — "let me review it",
  "show me before merging", or any such wording, which outranks how small the
  change looks — you have your answer (the review case omits the field). When
  they said neither, **ask, before filing**: one `AskUserQuestion`, proposing as
  the recommended option the narrowest policy that plausibly covers the deferred
  change, with "leave it for my review" as the alternative. A declined or
  unanswered question files with no `Automerge:` field — review is the safe
  default only after the owner had the chance to choose.

  **Start that proposal from the folder.** You are deferring a *specific*
  change, so you almost always know the tree it lands in — and a folder bound
  holds where a kind bound does not: `doc-changes` authorizes Markdown anywhere
  in the repo, the root `README.md` and `CLAUDE.md` included, where
  `under:docs` authorizes one tree. So propose `under:<that dir>`, intersected
  with the kind wherever the kind is known too — `under:docs && doc-changes`
  for a documentation edit, `under:<that dir> && comment-only-changes` for a
  comment pass in one place. Leave the scope bare where the change legitimately
  carries more than one kind: `under:src/auth` covers the fix *and* the test
  beside it, where intersecting a code class would park the moment the test
  file joined the diff. Reach for a bare kind class only where no single tree
  bounds the change, as a repo-wide comment sweep is `comment-only-changes`. And a
  change spanning several unrelated trees has no scope at all: propose review,
  never a policy widened until it fits.
- **`Task: <pack>/<task>`** — only when the deferral is a run of a *named task*
  rather than "implement this issue". Left out, the run is the built-in request
  implementer, which is what a `/do-later` almost always wants.

These ride the same block as the waits, on the body's first lines.

If the mark does not exist in the repository yet, it cannot be applied (the API
refuses an unknown label, and only the scheduler run creates it). Say so in your
reply and leave the issue filed — the label appears on the next scheduler run, and
the owner can mark it from the issue page.

## Then say what you filed

One line back to the owner: the issue link, what it waits on, the model family,
and whether it will merge itself or come back for approval.

A ruleTester case is a fixed cost paid over a thousand times in this suite:
makeRepo seeds a scratch repo, buildContext reads it, and between them that was
seventeen git subprocesses and 53ms before a single rule ran — the broad band
the per-test distribution is made of, not a few slow outliers.

Two of those seventeen spawns are the fixture's own content; the rest are
setup that is identical every time.

makeRepo now seeds ONE template repo per process and copies it. `git init` plus
the seed commit plus the feature branch produces a byte-identical tree for every
fixture whose `base` is empty, which is nearly all of them, and a file copy of
the result is ~3ms against ~27ms of subprocesses. The template is pruned of the
ten files git writes there and never reads back — the hook samples above all —
which was four fifths of the copy. A fixture with its own `base` files needs
them in the seed commit and still seeds the long way.

resolveBaseRef asked `rev-parse --verify` once per candidate and stopped at the
first hit, so a repo whose base is a local `main` — every check fixture, and any
clone with no remote — paid two misses on the `origin/` candidates before its
answer. `cat-file --batch-check` takes all four on stdin and answers each
independently through the same revision parser, `^{commit}` peeling included, in
one spawn. Verified to agree with rev-parse on every ambiguity that separates
them: a tag sharing a branch's name, a remote-tracking ref with no local branch,
both spellings present, and the canon checkout itself.

makeRepo 23.4ms -> 11.4ms, buildContext 28.9ms -> 23.3ms, a case 53.2ms ->
35.3ms. Proven behaviour-identical rather than assumed: the whole context —
every field, every file's contents, the added lines, the vendored set — hashes
the same through the old and new seeding paths across eight fixture shapes in
both scopes, including .gitignore/.gitattributes cases.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- committing: How a commit is cut — one concern per commit, the issue it references, a landed commit revised only by a new one, files staged by name. Use before any git commit.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- fetching-from-the-web: Reading a page or a file from the web in a session — exact bytes over a summarizing fetch, and what a 403 or an egress block means. Use before any WebFetch or curl, and when a fetch is denied.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and author the canon packs those facets earn. Use from a canon when a project's evidence shows a facet its shelf does not yet home — the curation stages' pack-writing method, and an owner's when asking what a project has taught the shelf.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.

- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- revalidating-rules: Re-probe the pack rules whose truth lives outside the repository — harness tool contracts, token reach, whether an MCP tool exists, a platform's behaviour — and correct the ones that have gone stale. - searching-for-a-tool: Finding a harness tool by name — the select form for a deferred tool, and what an empty search means. Use before any ToolSearch, and when a search finds nothing.

- writing-repo-scanning-checks: How a check that scans the repo picks its file set, strips comments before matching a forbidden token, and proves itself silent against real sources. Loaded for any edit of a coded or declared check.

Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.json or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.

You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.

When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. - artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.

For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. - simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.

TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). - security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- anthropic-skills:docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). - anthropic-skills:import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.

- anthropic-skills:pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. - anthropic-skills:xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. input.title: Sweep the remaining process.exit() calls that can truncate their own output
input.body:
Blocked-by: #2062
Model: opus
Automerge: under:engine

<!-- filed by /do-later -->

`process.exit()` over a **pipe** drops whatever is still queued on stdout/stderr. Every caller that *captures* a script's output gets a pipe — a test's `spawnSync`, a shell pipeline, an Actions step — and a Node pipe write is asynchronous, so under load the tail of the output is simply lost. Nothing reports it: the exit status was already decided, so the caller sees status 0 and a short answer.

This is measured, not theoretical. On `origin/main`, with six cores busy, **15 of 60** `check_the_world.mjs --list` callers got a catalog cut off at a row boundary, each missing the last 6-9 rules. It read as a flaky test for as long as anyone looked at it.

#2062 fixes the two check runners — `engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs` and `engine/checks/check_the_work.mjs` — by setting `process.exitCode` and letting the process end on its own, which flushes. This issue is the rest of the class.

## The work

Roughly 120 further `process.exit(` call sites under `engine/` and `packs/`. Not all of them are exposed: the hazard needs output written **before** the exit. Go through them and convert the ones that print, leaving the ones that do not.

Known exposed, in rough order of how much their output matters:

- `engine/selftest.mjs` — prints its summary and each failure, then exits. The rehearsal harness and the SessionStart hook both read that output.
- `engine/converge-wiring.mjs`
- `engine/migrations/apply.mjs`
- `engine/pack_loader/*.mjs` (`session-summary`, `run-pack-session-start`, `env-requirements`, `mount-skills`, `generate-skills-index`)
- `packs/claudinite-tasks/src/**`

`engine/hooks/hook-runner.mjs` and the judges are the deliberate exception named in the local pack's rules: a hook's exit code (0 or a deliberate 2) is the whole protocol, and `hook-runner.mjs` alone exits. Convert those only if their output is genuinely at risk, and say why in the diff.

## What done looks like

Each converted site sets `process.exitCode` and lets the process end. Where the exit was mid-script rather than the last statement, the control flow changes with it — an `if/else`, an early-returning `main()` — because an exit code does not stop the script the way `process.exit()` did. Watch for a call site whose exit is load-bearing *as a stop*.

Verify the way #2062 did rather than by reading: pick the converted entry point with the largest output, spawn it several dozen times from a `spawnSync` caller with the box loaded, and show the output complete every time where it was short before. `/tmp/.../repro-truncation.mjs` in that PR's session is the shape — a few dozen rounds against a CPU-starved box, counting the rows that came back.

The whole suite must stay green, and watch that nothing now hangs: a script that sets an exit code instead of forcing one will wait for the event loop to drain, so an open handle that `process.exit()` used to paper over becomes a hang. None of the converted runners showed one, but the wider set has not been checked.

## Ruled out

Do **not** land a check that greps for `process.exit(` — the corpus rules reject a check that asserts particular code still reads a particular way, and the legitimate exits (the hook protocol above all) would make it noise.

---

{"total_count":1,"workflow_runs":[{"id":34973138490,"name":"CI","display_title":"CI","workflow_id":317526095,"run_number":2021,"run_attempt":1,"event":"workflow_dispatch","status":"completed","conclusion":"success","head_branch":"claude/relaxed-meitner-pqhaq8","head_sha":"6517a7d3c213db3114fe1cfc60efd4acae699a87","head_commit":{"message":"Cut the git subprocesses every check fixture pays for

A ruleTester case is a fixed cost paid over a thousand times in this suite:
makeRepo seeds a scratch repo, buildContext reads it, and between them that was
seventeen git subprocesses and 53ms before a single rule ran — the broad band
the per-test distribution is made of, not a few slow outliers.

Two of those seventeen spawns are the fixture's own content; the rest are
setup that is identical every time.

makeRepo now seeds ONE template repo per process and copies it. `git init` plus
the seed commit plus the feature branch produces a byte-identical tree for every
fixture whose `base` is empty, which is nearly all of them, and a file copy of
the result is ~3ms against ~27ms of subprocesses. The template is pruned of the
ten files git writes there and never reads back — the hook samples above all —
which was four fifths of the copy. A fixture with its own `base` files needs
them in the seed commit and still seeds the long way.

resolveBaseRef asked `rev-parse --verify` once per candidate and stopped at the
first hit, so a repo whose base is a local `main` — every check fixture, and any
clone with no remote — paid two misses on the `origin/` candidates before its
answer. `cat-file --batch-check` takes all four on stdin and answers each
independently through the same revision parser, `^{commit}` peeling included, in
one spawn. Verified to agree with rev-parse on every ambiguity that separates
them: a tag sharing a branch's name, a remote-tracking ref with no local branch,
both spellings present, and the canon checkout itself.

makeRepo 23.4ms -> 11.4ms, buildContext 28.9ms -> 23.3ms, a case 53.2ms ->
35.3ms. Proven behaviour-identical rather than assumed: the whole context —
every field, every file's contents, the added lines, the vendored set — hashes
the same through the old and new seeding paths across eight fixture shapes in
both scopes, including .gitignore/.gitattributes cases.

input.body:
Ran the `ci-performance-evaluation` playbook end to end over this repo's suite. 3667 tests, all green.

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| **local suite wall clock** (4 cores) | 120.6s, 119.3s | **56.9s, 59.2s, 59.6s** |
| **CI `Unit tests` step** | 116s, 129s | **87s, 74s** |
| serial total, all 301 files | 263.3s | 209.4s |
| the longest single file | 76.5s | 22.4s |
| one `ruleTester` case | 53.2ms | 35.3ms |

CI gains less than local and its own spread is wide on both sides (116-129s before, 74-87s after), so the honest reading is ~1.5x there against ~2.1x here. I have not established the mechanism for the gap and am not going to guess at one — two samples an arm is what the numbers above are worth.

## Where the time actually was

The step breakdown first, over several runs: checkout 9-10s, setup-node 5s, **Unit tests 116-129s**, all three sweeps and both gates together ≤1s. The tests, and nothing else, were the job. No install step and no lockfile, so there is no cache to add.

Locally the suite ran 120.6s wall against 250s of user+sys on 4 cores — **52% utilisation, three cores idle**. Timing every file on its own found why: `vendoring/rehearsal/rehearsal.test.mjs` was **76.5s by itself**, and `node --test` parallelises across *files*. That one file was a floor no number of workers could get under, and it sat above the 66s that perfect 4-core parallelism would give — which is exactly why the suite idled at 120s.

Everything else was not slow tests but one fixed cost: ~1000 tests in a narrow band at ~53ms each, before any rule ran.

## What changed

**1. The rehearsals run concurrently.** The 74 (fixture, mode) rehearsals in that file each spend their wall clock waiting on nine child processes and share nothing — own temp dir, own subprocesses. `step()`/`buildFixture()` become async and the tests sit in a `describe` with a concurrency of 4. Steps *within* one rehearsal stay strictly ordered, each awaiting the last, because each judges what the one before wrote.

File alone **79.1s → 22.1s**. 4 is measured as the knee, not picked: 2 → 38.7s, 4 → 24.2s, 6 → 23.6s, 8 → 24.4s, and the 78.7s of CPU it now spends over 22.1s of wall is 3.6 of 4 cores. Proven still able to fail: pointing a step at a missing module turns the rehearsals red with the failing step's output intact.

**2. The per-fixture cost.** A `ruleTester` case was 17 git subprocesses before a single rule ran; two of them are the fixture's own content and the rest are identical every time.
- `makeRepo` seeds one template repo per process and copies it. `git init` + seed commit + feature branch is byte-identical for every fixture with an empty `base` — nearly all of them — and a file copy is ~3ms against ~27ms of subprocesses. The template is pruned of the ten files git writes there and never reads back (the hook samples above all), which was four fifths of the copy.
- `resolveBaseRef` asked `rev-parse --verify` once per candidate, so a repo based on a local `main` — every fixture, and any clone with no remote — paid two `origin/` misses before its answer. `cat-file --batch-check` answers all four on stdin in one spawn, through the same revision parser.

makeRepo 23.4ms → 11.4ms, buildContext 28.9ms → 23.3ms.

Behaviour-identical rather than assumed to be: the whole context — every field, file contents, added lines, the vendored set — hashes the same through both seeding paths across eight fixture shapes in both scopes; and `cat-file` agrees with `rev-parse` on every ambiguity that separates them (a tag sharing a branch's name, a remote ref with no local branch, both spellings present, the canon checkout itself).

## A real bug the faster suite surfaced

One A/B run went red on `--list emits the machine-readable rule catalog`. Not a flake: the catalog was cut off after the `t` rules, missing exactly the last 8. On **pristine `origin/main`**, with six cores busy, **15 of 60 `spawnSync` callers got a partial catalog** — status 0, empty stderr, a silently short answer on the channel whose whole purpose is being machine-read.

The cause is `process.exit()` over a pipe: every caller that *captures* output gets one, a Node pipe write is asynchronous, and `process.exit()` drops what is still queued. Both check runners now set `process.exitCode` and let the process end, which flushes; the world runner's branches become an if/else chain since an exit code does not stop the script, and the catalog goes out as one write. Under the identical load, **60 of 60 now return the full catalog**.

The same hazard sits on ~120 further `process.exit` call sites that print first — selftest, converge-wiring, the migration runner. That sweep is #2065 rather than widened into this PR.

## Left alone deliberately

- **Merging `buildContext`'s two `git diff --name-only` calls into one `--name-status`** — worth ~3ms a case, but the two disagree on rename entries in ways a fixture would not show, and that is not worth a subtle scoping bug.
- **Making `ctx.commits` / `ctx.branch` lazy** — another ~5ms a case. Real, but the suite is now within ~10% of its 4-core floor, so it buys single-digit seconds against a change to engine code every member runs.
- The 1562 tests that already run in under 1ms are 0.1% of the suite. They are fine, and this says so, so nobody re-profiles them.

| **local suite** (4 cores) | 120.6s, 119.3s | **56.9s, 59.2s, 59.6s** |
| **CI `Unit tests` step** | 116s, 129s | **87s, 74s** |

And a `ruleTester` case's 17 git subprocesses: `makeRepo` copies one pruned template repo instead of re-seeding (23.4→11.4ms), `resolveBaseRef` asks all four base-ref candidates in one `cat-file --batch-check` instead of up to four `rev-parse` calls.

The ~120 other call sites are [#2065](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/2065), automerging only inside `engine/` as you chose.

```
engine/checks/        the two runners exit by code so their output flushes; resolveBaseRef

engine-tests/         makeRepo seeds one template repo per process and copies it

[ADVISORY] ask-user-question-already-decided  (session) AskUserQuestion call #1
  a blocking question to the owner
  Why: a blocking question spends real human wall-clock, and most are already answered by an instruction in context, by state one read away, or by the recommended option being the status quo
  Fix: ask only a fork you cannot resolve yourself and batch every open decision into this one call; for anything answerable from the instruction or the tree, act and say what you assumed

[ADVISORY] sub-issue-without-parent  (session) mcp__github__issue_write call #1
  an issue filed under another ("Blocked-by: #2062") with no parent_issue_number
  Why: a child issue linked only by a number in its body leaves the parent blind to what is still open under it
  Fix: pass parent_issue_number on the create, or attach it afterwards with sub_issue_write (method add, sub_issue_id the id the create returned, not its number)

[ADVISORY] issue-labels-overwrite  (session) mcp__github__issue_write call #1
  an issue_write whose labels field replaces the issue's whole label set
  Why: issue_write's labels field replaces the issue's whole label set, so naming one label silently drops every other
  Fix: read the issue's current labels first and write back the full set with your one change applied

[ADVISORY] bare-sleep-wait  (session) Bash call #64
  a bare "; sleep 2;"
  Why: a padded sleep waits on nothing nameable; a guard that would not stand as the whole test is sleeping and calling it polling
  Fix: name the condition awaited — a run's status, a file's arrival, a deadline — and wait on that
